title: Measurement principles and field verification
summary: Foundational synthesis connecting measurement science, uncertainty, traceability, field observations, verification and fitness-for-purpose decisions. The page explicitly remains an initial conceptual model pending detailed technical review and worked examples.

relationships.note: Measurement principles underpin surveying observations and their interpretation.
Measurement uncertainty and quality concepts support positioning assessment.
Measurement and uncertainty concepts underpin propagation and sensitivity methods.

title: Coordinate transformation and CRS axis order
summary: Explains coordinate reference systems, axis order, coordinate operations and a bounded point-transformation implementation using PROJ/pyproj. High-accuracy operation selection, dynamic reference-frame epochs, vertical transformations and raster or geometry reprojection remain outside the stated scope.

relationships.note: Coordinate operations depend on geodetic reference-system definitions.
The lesson contributes to CRS selection, transformation and coordinate QA.

title: Geodetic coordinates, ECEF and the local ENU frame
summary: Explains the transformation chain from geodetic coordinates to Earth-Centred Earth-Fixed coordinates and a local East-North-Up frame, including the distinction between ellipsoid-normal Up and geocentric radial direction.

relationships.note: The coordinate frames rely on geodetic reference and ellipsoid definitions.
Local frames support field control and local engineering measurement contexts.

title: Helmert seven-parameter transformation in geocentric coordinates
summary: Describes a seven-parameter geocentric transformation using the Position Vector convention, including parameter units and the distinction from the Coordinate Frame convention. Parameter convention and transformation scope must remain explicit.

relationships.note: The transformation relates geocentric reference frames.
This is one geodetic computation method within the broader coordinate-transformation subject.

title: Uncertainty propagation and sensitivity implementation
summary: Documents dependency-free Python baselines for positional RMSE, Monte Carlo propagation under independent uniform inputs and first-/total-order Sobol sensitivity estimates. The package states important limitations including independent uniform inputs and no arbitrary correlated input distributions.

relationships.note: The package implements selected uncertainty propagation and sensitivity baselines.
Its interpretation depends on measurement and uncertainty concepts.

title: Classification, regression, retrieval and calibration metrics implementation
summary: Documents dependency-free metrics for classification, regression, retrieval and calibration, while explicitly excluding design-based area-adjusted accuracy and other specialised estimators. Pixel-count metrics must not be misrepresented as area-adjusted estimates where the sampling design requires weighting.

relationships.note: The package provides selected metrics used in spatial quality and accuracy assessment.

title: Measurement models and measurand definition
summary: Introduces operational measurand definition and measurement models, then develops a synthetic rectangular-area example showing first-order uncertainty propagation with and without correlated inputs. It is an educational module, not a field procedure or instrument specification.

relationships.note: A focused module within the broader measurement principles and field verification foundation.
Establishes the measurement model before uncertainty evaluation.
The worked example introduces covariance-aware propagation concepts.

title: Standard uncertainty: Type A and Type B evaluation
summary: Explains Type A and Type B as methods of evaluating standard uncertainty, covers repeated-observation statistics and distribution-based Type B evaluation, and combines components using a synthetic surveying distance budget with explicit assumptions and limitations.

relationships.note: A focused uncertainty-evaluation module within the broader measurement foundation.
Uses the measurement-model and measurand definitions established in the preceding module.
Connects uncertainty evaluation to the repository's uncertainty propagation implementation.

title: Covariance, correlated observations and generalized least squares
summary: Explains covariance and correlation, covariance matrices, shared observation errors, first-order propagation with correlated inputs and generalized least-squares adjustment. It uses the repository's synthetic Exercises D and K and does not prescribe a universal field covariance model.

relationships.note: A focused stochastic-modelling module within the broader measurement foundation.
Uses measurement models and input-quantity relationships.
Builds on standard uncertainty evaluation and combination.
Connects covariance-aware uncertainty propagation to the broader uncertainty-methods subject.

title: Covariance and generalized least-squares Python implementation
summary: Provides dependency-free covariance validation, session-common covariance construction, Cholesky-based unconstrained GLS and exact-constraint GLS using a KKT system. Includes tests and synthetic Exercise D and E examples. Both solvers require positive-definite observation covariance; constrained GLS additionally requires exact constraints that remove all datum defects. Singular-covariance generalized-inverse methods remain outside scope.

relationships.note: Implements covariance validation and covariance-aware linear uncertainty adjustment.
Implements the covariance and GLS concepts developed in the foundation module.
Builds on standard uncertainty and stochastic-model concepts.

title: Exact-constraint generalized least-squares Python implementation
summary: Extends the covariance/GLS implementation with exact linear constraints solved through a Lagrange-multiplier KKT system. A rank-deficient design can be handled when constraints remove all datum defects; observation covariance must still be positive definite. Includes synthetic datum-defect tests and explicit limitations.

relationships.note: Adds exact constraints to the existing covariance and GLS implementation.
Implements a constrained least-squares adjustment for datum-deficient linear models.
Builds on the covariance and generalized least-squares foundation.

title: Mathematical language, quantities and spatial models
summary: Introduces quantities, dimensions, units, variables, equations, functions, ratios, scale, sets, discrete and continuous representations, dimensional analysis and a disciplined workflow for constructing spatial mathematical models. Examples are illustrative and distinguish mathematical relationships from assumptions about real-world data and reference systems.

relationships.note: Opening module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Introduces vector and matrix language that is developed formally in linear algebra.
Introduces functions and relationships developed further in calculus.
Uses coordinate reference concepts to explain why coordinates require a defined reference.

title: Number systems, arithmetic and numerical representation
summary: Explains number sets, numeral bases, arithmetic with units, rounding, truncation, quantisation, significant figures, integer and floating-point storage, coordinate precision and raster scaling. Distinguishes numerical representation from measurement accuracy and uncertainty. Detailed floating-point error analysis and numerical stability are deferred to the numerical analysis foundation.

relationships.note: Second module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on mathematical language, quantities and spatial modelling.
Introduces finite numeric representation and defers numerical analysis to this foundation domain.
Connects reporting precision and resolution to measurement uncertainty.

title: Ratios, proportions, rates and logarithms
summary: Develops ratios, proportions, percentage and percentage-point change, direct and inverse proportionality, map scale, raster cell-area relationships, temporal rates, spatial density, compound growth, logarithms and decibel ratios. Worked examples and exercises emphasise denominator choice, units, reference quantities and limitations; specialised cartographic, statistical and signal-processing treatments remain in their respective foundations.

relationships.note: Third module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on the mathematical language, quantities and spatial modelling introduced in the first module.
Uses number systems and arithmetic conventions developed in the second module.
Introduces representative fraction and scale relationships; cartographic scale theory is developed in the cartography foundation.
Introduces logarithmic ratios and dynamic-range display contexts; radiometric theory is treated separately.
Introduces decibel ratios and logarithmic transformations; signal-processing theory is treated separately.

title: Equations, inequalities and mathematical reasoning
summary: Introduces algebraic expressions, equations, identities, rearrangement, dimensional consistency, linear and quadratic equations, systems, inequalities, absolute-value distance conditions, constraints, feasible sets and solution verification. Spatial examples illustrate threshold screening and distance models while distinguishing mathematical feasibility from real-world suitability. Matrix methods, advanced optimisation and geodetic distance computation remain outside scope.

relationships.note: Fourth module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Uses the variable, quantity, unit and model language introduced in the first module.
Builds on proportional relationships and mathematical modelling conventions.
Uses a circle and coordinate-axis intersection as an introductory geometric equation.
Highlights the need for an appropriate coordinate reference and distance model when applying spatial thresholds.
Connects numerical thresholds to measurement interpretation and uncertainty without treating a stipulated cutoff as a guarantee.

title: Functions and relationships in spatial science
summary: Defines functions through domains, codomains and ranges; develops common function types, injectivity, surjectivity, inverses and composition. Spatial examples include map scale, terrain surfaces, distance functions and coordinate mappings. Distinguishes deterministic, stochastic and empirical relationships and explains model-domain, unit, interpolation and extrapolation limitations.

relationships.note: Fifth module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Uses mathematical quantities, variables and spatial modelling language introduced in the first module.
Builds on equations and mathematical reasoning for evaluating and inverting function relationships.
Introduces coordinate mappings while reserving matrix transformations for the linear algebra foundation.
Introduces multivariable spatial functions while reserving derivatives and continuous change for calculus.
Uses geometric loci and Euclidean distance functions.
Frames coordinate reference transformations as mappings and distinguishes them from physical movement.
Distinguishes deterministic mappings from observation models and stochastic components.

title: Coordinate geometry and reference frames for spatial science
summary: Develops Cartesian coordinates, planar and three-dimensional distance, midpoints, lines, intersections, circles, planes, geometric loci and simple local-frame translations. Explains why coordinate tuples require frame, units and CRS metadata, and distinguishes planar Cartesian calculations from geographic coordinates and Earth-surface distance. Detailed geodesy, matrix transformations and numerical robustness are reserved for their dedicated foundations.

relationships.note: Sixth module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on functions and mappings to describe coordinate-based geometric relationships.
Introduces coordinate-frame changes while reserving matrix representations and rotations for linear algebra.
Introduces lines, planes, circles, distances and geometric loci.
Explains the distinction between Cartesian coordinates, geographic coordinates and geodetic reference systems.
Notes that map projections distort geometric properties and that planar map measurements require projection-aware interpretation.
Connects coordinate-derived geometry to input measurement quality and uncertainty.
Identifies finite precision, rounding and geometric numerical robustness as separate numerical-analysis concerns.

title: Vectors and vector operations for spatial science
summary: Introduces scalars, points and vectors; components, magnitude, displacement, addition, scalar multiplication, unit vectors, dot and cross products, projection and parametric lines. Spatial examples connect vectors to movement, directional fields, terrain and coordinate observations. Formal vector spaces, matrices and differential operators are reserved for linear algebra and calculus.

relationships.note: Seventh module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on coordinate geometry and reference frames to interpret coordinate differences and directions.
Uses function notation for spatial vector fields and terrain relationships.
Introduces vector operations while reserving abstract vector spaces and matrix representations for linear algebra.
Introduces the gradient connection while reserving differential operators for calculus.
Uses Euclidean geometry, angles, perpendicularity and areas.
Highlights the need for compatible coordinate frames when subtracting positions and representing directions.
Connects coordinate residuals and observed displacements to measurement interpretation without equating residuals with true errors.

title: Sequences, series and approximation for spatial science
summary: Introduces sequences, recursive updates, arithmetic and geometric sequences, limits, convergence, series, partial sums and elementary approximation. Spatial examples connect discretisation to raster resolution, curve approximation, iterative stopping criteria and time-stepped simulation. Distinguishes convergence from accuracy and numerical approximation from measurement uncertainty; advanced convergence and numerical stability are reserved for specialist foundations.

relationships.note: Eighth module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Uses vector norms and spatial vector examples when introducing iterative vector estimates.
Connects sequences and limits to later calculus treatment.
Distinguishes deterministic sequences from stochastic processes.
Separates approximation error from measurement uncertainty.
Connects repeated updates and discretisation to algorithmic processes.
Introduces convergence and approximation while reserving numerical stability and error analysis for numerical analysis.
Connects spatial discretisation and representation choices to geographic information.

title: Mathematical modelling and dimensional analysis for spatial science
summary: Introduces a reusable spatial model-building workflow, distinguishes real systems, questions, data, conceptual and mathematical models, algorithms and outputs, and develops variables, parameters, constraints, dimensional homogeneity, SI unit conversion, scaling, sensitivity and plausibility checks. Worked examples are hypothetical; uncertainty propagation, geodesy, calculus, optimisation and numerical stability remain in specialist foundations.

relationships.note: Ninth module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on mathematical language, quantities, units and introductory spatial models.
Uses numerical representation and arithmetic with units.
Uses ratios, rates and scaling relationships.
Uses equations, constraints and mathematical reasoning.
Connects model inputs and measurands to measurement science without duplicating uncertainty evaluation.
Highlights coordinate-reference and geodetic requirements for spatial distance and area.
Defers numerical conditioning, floating-point error and stability to numerical analysis.

title: Trigonometry for spatial science
summary: Introduces planar angle conventions and units, radians, right-triangle trigonometry, the unit circle, inverse functions, periodicity, bearings and azimuths, coordinate components, slope and circular geometry. Worked examples and exercises use idealised local Cartesian geometry. Geodetic azimuths, ellipsoidal calculations, instrument procedures, projection distortion and measurement uncertainty remain in specialist foundations.

relationships.note: Tenth module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on coordinate geometry and reference frames.
Uses vector components and direction.
Distinguishes local planar angle conventions from geodetic azimuths and Earth-referenced calculations.
Connects angular quantities to measurement science without claiming instrument procedures or uncertainty evaluation.
Supports planar geometric constructions and coordinate calculations.
Provides elementary angular language for sensor geometry; full sensor models remain specialist.
Provides trigonometric prerequisites for optics and wave physics.

title: Introductory discrete mathematics and logic for spatial science
summary: Introduces discrete and continuous representations, sets and set operations, Cartesian products, relations and their properties, equivalence relations, functions, propositions, connectives, truth tables, predicates, quantifiers, Boolean query logic, introductory graph vocabulary, proof and counterexample methods, and mathematical induction. Spatial examples cover feature selection, quality rules, topology, classifications and networks. Advanced graph theory, formal logic, combinatorics, database-specific semantics and algorithm analysis remain specialist topics.

relationships.note: Eleventh module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on equations, inequalities and mathematical reasoning.
Uses functions and relationships as mathematical mappings.
Provides prerequisites for algorithmic conditions, data structures and formal correctness.
Provides set, relation and predicate language for geographic information and spatial queries.
Connects formal relations and graph structures to geometry.
Introduces relations and partitions while reserving topological theory for its specialist foundation.
Provides graph vocabulary used in network optimisation and operations research.

title: Application coverage audit — mathematics for spatial science
summary: Desk-based curriculum audit of mathematics Modules 01–11 against eight representative spatial workflows: local traverse, GIS selection, raster analysis, terrain, networks, site screening, field/sensor data collection and temporal modelling. Distinguishes introductory coverage from specialist prerequisites and defines six targeted revisions. Not a field trial, learner assessment, independent peer review or technical certification.

relationships.note: Assesses the introductory mathematics sequence against representative spatial applications.

title: Vectors, matrices and linear transformations
summary: Introduces scalar, vector and matrix notation; dimensions; vector and matrix operations; linear combinations; matrix-vector products; linear transformations; planar rotation; affine transformations and homogeneous coordinates. Spatial connections include coordinate operations, observation/design matrices and multivariate data. Full linear-system theory, subspaces, rank, least squares, spectral methods and numerical analysis are deferred to later modules or specialist foundations.

relationships.note: First module in the linear algebra and matrix methods foundation domain.
Extends introductory vector components into matrix operations and linear transformations.
Introduces matrix notation for planar coordinate operations while deferring geodetic reference-frame and CRS operation theory.
Introduces design-matrix notation used in observation models without duplicating measurement uncertainty theory.
Introduces matrix representation and composition used in computational methods.

title: Linear combinations, span, independence and subspaces
summary: Explains linear combinations, span, subspaces, linear independence and dependence, uniqueness of representation and the column-space interpretation of a matrix. Spatial applications distinguish parameter-direction independence from observation redundancy, precision and reliability. Numerical rank, conditioning, full identifiability analysis and least-squares estimation are deferred.

relationships.note: Second module in the linear algebra and matrix methods foundation domain.
Builds on vector, matrix and linear-transformation notation.
Introduces vector-space ideas used to reason about observation models and network geometry without replacing measurement science.
Provides algebraic prerequisites for matrix algorithms and computational rank analysis.
Supports understanding of independent model directions and feasible representations in optimisation.

title: Linear systems, elimination, rank and null spaces
summary: Introduces matrix-form linear systems, elementary row operations, augmented matrices, Gaussian elimination, pivots, exact matrix rank, null spaces, rank–nullity, consistency and solution uniqueness. A synthetic two-point relative-height network demonstrates a common-translation datum defect and its removal by an explicit datum constraint. Numerical rank, conditioning, least squares, stochastic adjustment and advanced constraint theory are deferred.

relationships.note: Third module in the linear algebra and matrix methods foundation domain.
Uses matrix and linear-transformation notation.
Uses span, independence and column-space concepts to interpret rank and solution structure.
Connects rank and null spaces to a simplified relative-height network and datum defect.
Distinguishes exact algebraic rank from numerical rank and conditioning, which require numerical analysis.

title: Bases, dimension, coordinates and change of basis
summary: Explains bases as independent spanning sets, dimension, coordinate columns, basis matrices and conversion between coordinate representations. Includes a non-orthogonal basis example, a rotated orthonormal frame, and the distinction between vector basis changes and point-coordinate translations. Clarifies why general CRS and geodetic coordinate operations are broader than a constant linear basis conversion.

relationships.note: Fourth module in the linear algebra and matrix methods foundation domain.
Uses vectors, matrices and linear transformations.
Uses span, independence and subspace concepts to define a basis.
Builds on dimension, rank and solution structure.
Basis and coordinate-frame concepts support, but do not replace, geodetic reference-system and CRS operation theory.

title: Inner products, norms, orthogonality and projections
summary: Introduces real inner-product spaces, Euclidean dot products, induced norms, angles, Cauchy–Schwarz, orthogonality, Gram matrices for non-orthonormal bases, projections onto directions and subspaces, and the orthogonality condition underlying ordinary least squares. Synthetic spatial examples cover displacement length, along-/cross-track decomposition and closest point on a finite segment. Geodetic metrics, weighted estimation and numerical algorithms are deferred.

relationships.note: Fifth module in the linear algebra and matrix methods foundation domain.
Uses vector and matrix operations.
Uses basis-coordinate representations and Gram matrices.
Projection geometry supports point-to-line and point-to-segment computational geometry.
Residual orthogonality gives a geometric interpretation of least-squares fitting, while measurement quality and uncertainty require separate models.
Computational projection and least-squares solvers require numerical methods beyond the geometric derivation.

title: Least squares and constrained systems
summary: Develops linear observation models, ordinary least squares, residual orthogonality, normal equations, rank and identifiability, weighted least squares, generalized least squares with correlated observations, exact linear constraints and the KKT system. Uses synthetic line-fitting and relative-height datum examples. Distinguishes exact datum conventions from stochastic external control and links the derivation to the repository's constrained/unconstrained GLS implementation and survey-adjustment learning path.

relationships.note: Sixth module in the linear algebra and matrix methods foundation domain.
Uses rank, null spaces and datum-defect concepts.
Uses projection and residual orthogonality geometry.
Applies estimation to measurement networks while distinguishing datum conventions, control and stochastic uncertainty.
Stable numerical least-squares solution requires appropriate matrix factorizations and conditioning analysis.
Least-squares estimation is a quadratic optimisation problem with linear equality constraints.

title: Symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and definiteness
summary: Explains real symmetric matrices, quadratic forms, positive/negative definiteness and semidefiniteness, eigenvalue and principal-minor criteria, Cholesky structure, covariance matrices as positive-semidefinite quadratic forms, variance of linear combinations, least-squares curvature, Mahalanobis distance, uncertainty ellipses and convex quadratic objectives. Includes worked synthetic examples, exercises and explicit numerical/statistical limitations.

relationships.note: Seventh module in the linear algebra and matrix methods foundation domain.
Uses inner products, norms and orthogonality.
Develops the quadratic objective and curvature underlying least squares and GLS.
Covariance matrices encode variances of linear combinations of random variables.
Covariance and quadratic forms support uncertainty propagation and measurement adjustment.
Positive definiteness and matrix factorizations affect numerical solution methods.
Definiteness determines convexity and curvature of quadratic optimisation objectives.

title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and spectral structure
summary: Introduces eigenvalues and eigenvectors, characteristic equations, orthogonal diagonalisation and the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices, Rayleigh quotient, covariance eigenstructure, principal directions and uncertainty ellipses, covariance and correlation PCA, selected graph spectral concepts, and repeated linear transformations. Includes worked synthetic examples and exercises, and distinguishes symmetric spectral results from nonsymmetric spatial weights and general operators.

relationships.note: Eighth module in the linear algebra and matrix methods foundation domain.
Uses symmetric matrices, definiteness and covariance quadratic forms.
Covariance eigenstructure underlies variance directions and covariance-based PCA.
Spectral methods connect to spatial dependence and selected spatial-statistical operators.
Practical eigenanalysis depends on numerical algorithms, conditioning and approximation methods.
Graph and spatial-weights operators can be studied spectrally, subject to their symmetry and construction.

title: Matrix factorizations: LU, QR, Cholesky and singular-value decomposition
summary: Explains pivoted LU, QR and orthogonal least-squares solution, Cholesky for symmetric positive-definite systems, singular-value decomposition, numerical rank, null directions and the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. Connects factorization choice to GLS whitening, PCA, measurement-network datum defects and numerical modelling cautions. Includes worked examples, selection guidance and exercises.

relationships.note: Ninth module in the linear algebra and matrix methods foundation domain.
Uses least-squares objectives, residual orthogonality and constrained estimation.
Uses spectral structure and singular directions.
Factorizations support covariance-aware estimation and measurement-network solutions.
Numerical stability, conditioning, rank thresholds and solver selection are developed further in scientific computing.
QR and related methods support least-squares optimisation.

title: Covariance matrices and multivariate structure
summary: Develops covariance and correlation matrices, positive-semidefinite structure, variance of linear combinations, covariance propagation under linear and first-order nonlinear transformations, GLS covariance, spatial uncertainty geometry, covariance and correlation PCA, Mahalanobis distance, and the finite-matrix connection to spatial covariance functions. Includes synthetic worked examples, exercises and explicit scope boundaries.

relationships.note: Tenth module in the linear algebra and matrix methods foundation domain.
Uses positive-semidefinite quadratic forms and covariance matrix structure.
Uses spectral decomposition to interpret principal directions and PCA.
Uses Cholesky factorization and matrix transformations for covariance-aware computation.
Probability and statistical inference develop random-vector distributions and covariance estimation.
Spatial statistics develops spatial covariance functions, random fields and geostatistical inference.
Measurement science interprets covariance in uncertainty propagation and correlated observations.

title: Matrix factorization computational companion
summary: Runnable NumPy and SciPy comparison of pivoted LU for square systems, QR for least squares, Cholesky whitening for a synthetic correlated-observation GLS example, and SVD for near-dependency and PCA. Includes tests, reproducibility instructions, method-selection guidance and explicit numerical/statistical limitations. Demonstrates library routines rather than reimplementing production factorization algorithms.

relationships.note: Computational companion to the matrix factorization foundation module.
Uses Cholesky whitening and SVD/PCA in covariance and multivariate examples.
Numerical analysis covers conditioning, stability, precision and solver selection in greater depth.
GLS example illustrates covariance-aware weighting under an explicitly assumed synthetic covariance.

title: Integrated synthetic spatial case: affine control and terrain estimation
summary: Integrates pivoted LU affine control transformation, QR terrain-plane least squares, Cholesky whitening for GLS under an explicitly assumed correlated-error covariance, and SVD numerical-rank diagnostics in one deterministic synthetic spatial workflow. Includes a runnable script, tests, diagnostics and strict scope limitations.

relationships.note: Applies LU, QR, Cholesky and SVD roles together in a single spatial workflow.
Uses an explicit covariance model for GLS whitening and interprets numerical rank of the whitened design.
Demonstrates a synthetic control-to-terrain estimation chain without claiming survey adjustment or field accuracy.
Reports conditioning, singular values, numerical-rank tolerance and solver-specific diagnostics.

title: Practical exercise: affine control and covariance-aware terrain estimation
summary: Staged learner exercise and worked interpretation for the integrated synthetic spatial factorization case. Tasks cover affine control and LU, QR terrain-plane estimation, Cholesky whitening and GLS, SVD numerical rank and conditioning, covariance critique, real-world validity checks and a 20-point marking guide.

relationships.note: Turns the integrated synthetic spatial implementation into a learner-facing exercise and worked interpretation.
Assesses the selection and interpretation of LU, QR, Cholesky and SVD.
Assesses covariance structure, GLS weighting and multivariate numerical interpretation.
Uses a synthetic control-to-terrain estimation scenario while explicitly separating it from field survey evidence.

title: Photogrammetric image acquisition: geometry, control and quality assurance
summary: Initial learning unit on designing photogrammetric image observations before processing. Covers image formation, GSD versus accuracy, footprint and overlap calculations, ray geometry, camera and platform effects, scene conditions, tie points, ground control, independent checks and acquisition QA. Includes a hypothetical planning exercise and links to a bounded flight-design calculator; specialist review and field validation remain outstanding.

relationships.note: Develops acquisition principles for photogrammetry and structure from motion.
Connects airborne optical image capture to remote-sensing acquisition.
Applies measurement quality, control, uncertainty and independent validation concepts.

title: Photogrammetric mapping: project-to-validated-deliverable recipe
summary: A project-level photogrammetry workflow connecting requirements, reconnaissance and feasibility, sensor and image geometry design, control/check planning, field acquisition, raw-data preservation, processing, internal diagnostics, independent validation and delivery. Includes a reusable project record and QA checklist. It is desk-designed and not field-tested, specialist-reviewed or jurisdictionally approved.

relationships.note: Turns the image-acquisition principles into an end-to-end project workflow.
Provides a practical photogrammetric mapping workflow within the photogrammetry and 3D reconstruction recipe family.
Operationalises photogrammetric image acquisition and control.
Uses measurement quality, traceability and independent verification principles.

title: Probability models, events and conditioning
summary: Introduces probability spaces, events, probability rules, marginal and joint probabilities, conditional probability, independence, disjointness, total probability and Bayes' theorem. Uses an original synthetic spatial-screening example to show how prevalence changes positive predictive value, and makes the sampling unit, unequal-area weighting and spatial-dependence assumptions explicit.

relationships.note: Initial module in the probability and statistical inference foundation domain.
Uses sets, functions, ratios and mathematical notation introduced in mathematics for spatial science.
Probability models later extend to random vectors and covariance structures represented with linear algebra.
Introduces dependence generally; spatial dependence and random fields are developed in the spatial statistics foundation.
Probability is used in measurement uncertainty, but does not replace measurand definition or metrological traceability.
